title: What Does China Want?
author: Jessica Chen Weiss
text: Podcast What Does China Want?A Conversation With Jessica Chen Weiss Published on September 3, 2026 Play Listen to the Episode 52 minutes 00:00 / 51:59 0.5×1×1.5×2× MP3 Close audio player Print Print this article Save Sign in and save to read later Close Share What Does China Want? A Conversation With Jessica Chen Weiss Share in email Share on Facebook Share on X Share on LinkedIn Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/what-does-china-wanthttps://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/what-does-china-want Request reprint permissions here.Episode Details There has been no shortage of dizzying shifts in American foreign policy since Donald Trump returned to the White House last year. But perhaps none have been as surprising as the shift on China. In his first term, Trump helped create a hard-line consensus centered on fears of a growing threat. Now, he seems much more interested in striking deals—as he presumably will be when Xi Jinping comes to Washington later this month.Many analysts of U.S. China policy have reacted to this reversal with dismay. But Jessica Chen Weiss sees it as an opportunity to forge a more sensible approach. Weiss, a professor and the faculty director of the Institute for America, China, and the Future of Global Affairs at Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies and a former State Department official, has warned of the dangers of zero-sum thinking about China in a series of essays for Foreign Affairs. Her most recent essay, in the September/October issue, focuses on the myth and the reality of China’s critical mineral dominance.Dan Kurtz-Phelan spoke to Weiss on August 31 about what China wants—which is also the title of her forthcoming book—and what U.S. foreign policy can do to meet those ambitions without resorting to dangerous confrontation.Sources:“How China Found Its Most Potent Weapon” by Gloria Xiong and Jessica Chen WeissWhat China Wants by Jessica Chen Weiss“The China Trap” by Jessica Chen Weiss“The Case Against the China Consensus” by Jessica Chen Weiss“A World Safe for Autocracy?” by Jessica Chen WeissInstitute for America, China, and the Future of Global Affairs at Johns Hopkins SAIS“The Cost of Keeping China Out” by Peter Cowhey and Meg Rithmire“Taiwan and the True Sources of Deterrence” by Bonnie S. Glaser, Jessica Chen Weiss, and Thomas J. ChristensenThis episode of The Foreign Affairs Interview was produced by Adelaide Parker, Ben Metzner, and Kanishk Tharoor, with audio engineering by Todd Yeager and original music by Robin Hilton. Special thanks to Irina Hogan.This is a rough transcript of the conversation. Please consult the underlying audio prior to citation.DAN KURTZ-PHELANJessica, it’s wonderful to have you back on the podcast. It’s been a few years.JESSICA CHEN WEISSGreat to be here as always.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIf we’d been having this conversation, I think even 18 months ago, I think it’s safe to say that we both would’ve agreed that a hard line on China was one of the few matters of real bipartisan consensus in Washington. That formulation was so obvious at that point that it had become fairly hackneyed, I would say. In Donald Trump’s second term, that seeming consensus has come apart pretty quickly and dramatically. How has that made you think differently about the nature of what seemed to be a consensus for several years? Was it always less solid than it seemed through the latter part of Trump’s first term and the Biden presidency, or is there something else going on?JESSICA CHEN WEISSWell, I think that the consensus has come apart in ways that I didn’t anticipate, although I think I wrote for Foreign Affairs on the eve of that election that the consensus was shallower and more wobbly than it appeared. There was a shared concern about many of China’s actions and American standing in the world, but there was far less agreement on exactly the shape of that challenge and what exactly the appropriate American response should be aiming at. And that said, of course, I certainly didn’t predict all that has happened since. I think that President Trump has taken it in directions that would’ve been hard to imagine just a year and a half ago. But he has, I think, very much demonstrated that that consensus was not as constraining as his predecessor and the Biden administration seems to believe.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIt was interesting for me in this context to go back and read the piece you published in Foreign Affairs in 2022. It was called “The China Trap,” and it was quite notable at the time because of the way it pushed against that hard line. At its center was a warning about how the fixation on the challenge from China was warping U.S. policy. I’ll just read one line that really captured it. You wrote, quote, “The current course will not just bring indefinite deterioration of the U.S.-Chinese relationship and a growing danger of catastrophic conflict. It also threatens to undermine the sustainability of American leadership in the world and the vitality of American society and democracy at home.”So quite a resounding warning. As you reflect on the arc of American policy and the American debate on China in the last four years, do you think those warnings, which again seemed fairly lonely at the time, have become heated? Is that what sunk into the system?JESSICA CHEN WEISSI think there are a couple things have happened. One, I think the number of Americans who agreed that the United States and China were far too close to the precipice of an actual war in the Asia-Pacific or an economic meltdown as last year’s trade war and export control war demonstrated. And that actually public opinion has shifted in the direction of wanting to resolve conflicts with China through one survey called cooperation and not through containing China’s influence. I think the second thing is that China has not been meaningfully slowed by many of the measures that were endorsed on a bipartisan basis, that efforts to slow China down may have constricted China’s access to compute, for example, but they’ve been very effective indigenizing and finding other ways to accelerate China’s modernization and development of essentially just as effective a tech stack as the one that we have an offer.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAnd you mean there are the export controls on chips along with sanctions and tariffs and everything else that was meant to restrain China’s growth?JESSICA CHEN WEISSExactly. I mean, I think the heart of the Biden administration strategy was premised on this idea that there would be a small yard and a high fence and that the way in which the United States would maintain its security was by staying ever ahead of China. But what ahead really looked like, and then maybe you could say that they succeeded on the metrics that they specified, which was to say at the model layer of these artificial intelligence models. But in other ways in the adoption of AI technology and open source, China has really flourished. Chinese companies have flourished. But that’s a little bit too in the weeds. I think more broadly, I think there’s been a recognition that the United States needs to do better on its own terms rather than simply beating China at China’s game. In some ways, maybe it’s too late to contain China, constrain China.And then though, I think the debate has not yet settled on what the alternative should be. Should it be a withdrawing into a fortress America or should it be one that is allied, scale, friendshoring, or is it one that actually does need to continue to some degree maintain a degree of integration with China, including selective openness in the words of Meg Rithmire and Peter Cowhey, who recently wrote a piece that I endorse, where it’s not just enough to go it alone or even go it alone with allies and partners. We actually need many of the technologies that China is pioneering in order if we want to achieve our own objectives in terms of affordability and decarbonization.So I think that’s yet a different prescription. And again, we need more of this kind of debate. I don’t think that the answer is obvious and these are genuinely hard questions, which is one of the reasons why I came back to Washington after writing that 2022 piece and started the Institute for America, China and the Future of Global Affairs, ACF at Johns Hopkins SAIS to bring together these different perspectives and tackle these really hard policy trade-offs.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI won’t ask you to endorse, let alone describe all elements of Trump’s China policy because that’s probably impossible to do. But as you’ve looked at the surprising directions he’s gone in, to use your formulation, what do you think he’s getting wrong and what do you think he’s getting right?JESSICA CHEN WEISSLet me start with what he’s getting right. I think that he’s getting right the fact that we do need a stable and constructive relationship with China. And the two presidents, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, agreed to that in his visit this spring to Beijing. That’s about where it lands. I think that the actual implementation and the degree of strategic thinking and coherence underneath that, I would be pleased to be shown wrong and that the upcoming summit at the end of September will demonstrate a great deal of strategic foresight. But I think the challenge has been one of distraction and under preparation. And, of course, that kind of in symmetry and in diplomatic engagement was preceded by some of the most extreme threats and tariffs against China, followed quickly by desire for a truce, recognizing that neither side could really sustain the level of economic damage that the actions and retaliations were going to bring about.And I think that unfortunately there’s been a missed opportunity. The president has been clearly willing to say unprecedented things about our allies and partners in the Asia-Pacific, including his comments about Taiwan. After making the largest ever arms sale, then postponed an arms sale and said he would treat it as a bargaining chip. I think the previous presidents and probably most of Capitol Hill feel, I think, quite trapped by the fear of looking weak or insufficiently committed to the principle of Taiwan’s defense. Trump feels no such compunction, but neither has he shown that he’s willing to get something for what he’s giving. And so this willingness to make what are apparently unilateral concessions without a real strategic conversation about the concessions that China needs to make in return, I think is a real missed opportunity and is not setting us up for success on that dimension.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIf you were advising the president—it’s a hard thing to imagine, but let’s say you are—what kinds of concessions do you think you should be asking for in the upcoming summit?JESSICA CHEN WEISSWell, I think that, I mean, of course these need to be mutual because long gone are the days where the United States could demand things and China would be forced to give them up. But there are other things that the United States has put on the table, including this question of arms sales to Taiwan. I know that’s not a popular viewpoint, but I do think that asking that China, in exchange for this continued pause, pull back its military operations across the center line of the Taiwan Strait, many of the things that we, along with Bonnie Glaser and Tom Christensen argued for, is that assurances from the Chinese side are necessary in order to prevent this action-reaction spiral from escalating. And so we’ve seen a lot of sort of assurances on the United States side. I hesitate to call them fully assurances. It’s hard to know exactly what was delivered privately, and comments to Fox News are not the kinds of off-the-cuff remarks we would’ve advised. But nonetheless, there does need to be this balance struck and I worry we’ve over-corrected in the other direction.I mean, the other thing is that President Trump, unlike much of the Republican Party and others in his administration, has signaled his openness to welcoming Chinese students, that he said it’s good for American universities. But the administration is doing anything but presenting a welcoming face to international students and scholars. And so this is not a concession per se, but this is an area, this growing estrangement between the two societies, that makes it really difficult even to understand what’s happening in the other country, let alone benefit from the human talent that really wants to leave China and go elsewhere. Unfortunately, we’ve made it increasingly difficult for those who want to stay in the United States to contribute. So I don’t know where that’s going, but that’s an area, the restoration or stabilization of, we call people-to-people ties, would be a really important area, I think, to make some progress towards stabilizing the relationship.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou spend a fair amount of time speaking to Chinese scholars and analysts and officials and reading Chinese sources. What is the debate about Trump’s China policy among Chinese voices at this point? How are they understanding where things are and what that means for the relationship?JESSICA CHEN WEISSI think a lot of them are wondering just how durable this is. After the midterms or leading into 2028, will there be a snapback whether it’s because Trump himself authorizes a more confrontational turn as he did in his first administration? You’ll recall that it wasn’t until COVID hit in 2020 that the Trump administration unleashed a whole range of really harsh measures and also really escalated the rhetoric against the Chinese Communist Party. You remember a variety of speeches by senior Trump administration figures. So there’s a real question as to whether or not this framework can endure. I think that the Chinese side is interested. I think they do prefer stability to growing confrontation, and I think that’s part of the reason why they pulled back or were willing to pull back in a truce last spring and last fall rather than trying to crush the U.S. economy as they could have had they maintained the really harsh restrictions on the export of critical minerals, rare earths and permanent magnets. So I think that’s one question.I think the other question is, now that the United States is not playing such a leading role on the world stage, what role does China want to play? Speaking to one China expert who often advises the government, he said that China has been like a student trying to graduate and very, very focused. And I guess the analogy was to resisting what was felt as U.S. pressure, this constrainment, encirclement, et cetera. And now that that has been to some extent lifted, or China feels that it has fought back and been able to fight the United States to a standstill, now what? Now that China in this metaphor or analogy has graduated, there’s a whole range of choices available and there are real trade-offs, and how to evaluate those trade-offs and what policies to pursue is an open question.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI want to pick up that big question about what China wants and how it sees its role in the world, but I first want to focus on the rare earths and critical minerals back and forth that started in April or May of 2025. This is the subject of your most recent piece in Foreign Affairs with Gloria Xiong called “How China Found Its Most Potent Weapon.” What was most striking to me in watching that back and forth is just how surprised people in Washington seem to be by the effectiveness of that tool. Were you surprised by how the Chinese deployed and how the U.S. reacted?JESSICA CHEN WEISSI think that it was something that there had been warning signs, but it wasn’t unleashed fully until the Trump administration’s wild escalation. But it wasn’t even the tariffs, it was actually the export controls and their expansion that led China to unveil its own extraterritorial set of export controls.DAN KURTZ-PHELANMeaning that it was not just restricting what the critical minerals and related products that it would send to others, but it was preventing anyone from using those products from sending it to the U.S. or other markets that China didn’t like.JESSICA CHEN WEISSExactly, exactly. Although there had been warnings, I think especially from industry when under the Biden administration, after the imposition of export controls on advanced chips and manufacturing equipment, China retaliated with some restrictions on critical minerals, but hadn’t gone to the extent that it did later. And I think that at the time, I think some U.S. analysts observed that China hadn’t really gone for the big guns yet. And I think that that led many to believe that this was going to be okay, that China was responding with relative restraint. And I think in this narrative, it was really the Trump administration’s fault in 2025 that China reached for its quote-unquote “break glass playbook.”And it’s true that what set in motion China’s effort to build out and consider a more expansive use of export controls on rare earths was the first Trump administration’s actions against Huawei. But they had been planning and learning from U.S. export controls and sanctions, financial sanctions, studying and trying to figure out, because they understood that these could also be counterproductive, that they could accelerate a process of diversification away from China. And in fact, and also of course lead to retaliation that China might not be prepared to withstand. And so, it was really over three successive U.S. administrations that China first really decided to embrace this, explored it, prepared for it, and then finally unleashed it.And so, in some sense, it was a very dramatic turn of events. And I do think that one of the—and this is something that Henry Farrell has pointed out in a recent piece for ACF—that often you don’t realize where the pain points are and just how significant they are until you force the target to activate them. And so, I don’t think we really understood just how much—the industries may have understood—but often these supply chains are quite opaque, and so we didn’t quite understand how acute and painful the stoppage of Chinese rare earth exports and permanent magnets would be until it happened.DAN KURTZ-PHELANSo while some of this is about the rather slipshod policymaking process in the Trump administration, you think the problem goes much deeper than that in American strategic circles?JESSICA CHEN WEISSIt’s not just the strategic circles. I mean, it’s the top-to-bottom understanding of despite the rhetoric of decoupling and de-risking, we remain highly interdependent and that in this context or the belief in escalation dominance, that we have it and they’re just going to fold like Secretary Bessent said at the outset of the trade war, that China holds a pair of twos and so we can force them to back off. That just doesn’t really capture reality. And so, I think that rather than pursuing or now having realized the extent of our vulnerability to believe that we could either fully insulate ourselves or then find the new ace card that the United States could play is really foolhardy as a strategic objective and that what we should instead be focused more on is developing what Dalip Singh called a shared doctrine of restraint.DAN KURTZ-PHELANThe core argument of the recent essay is about the way that China found its way to dominance over the rare earths and critical mineral supply chain. You argue that, and I’ll quote you here, “That even though China has sought to take advantage of its position, its dominance is not the result of a grand farsighted scheme to hold the world hostage.” I think it’s probably worth saying a bit about just how dominant China is at this particular moment, what gave it such leverage when it launched these controls last year, but also how you see the right way of understanding the history of how we got here. And perhaps just as importantly, why it matters to understand those intentions, it’s not just a matter of academic debate.JESSICA CHEN WEISSAbsolutely. So China dominates the vast majorities, like 80 to 85 percent, especially of permanent magnets made with these rare earth minerals. And that dominance, there’s little sign of abating it, especially in key rare earths such as yttrium, where it’s not even clear on what date that might be reduced, the dependence on China as a sole source. And it’s not that rare earths are that rare, it’s just that they rarely appear in minable concentrations around the world and it’s incredibly polluting as well. And so, by the 1990s, China had really become a favored location for their production because the developed countries, it was both incredibly polluting and also less expensive to just send it over to China.And so the market shifted and some look at this as a deliberate effort by China to starve the world, something that China has been plotting ever since Deng Xiaoping said in the early 1990s that the Middle East has oil, China has rare earths. But that actually reflected . . . his quote in particular, I think took place at around the time of the end of the first Gulf War, when China and China’s strategic experts realized the extent to which they were vulnerable and that key resources could be a source of conflict. And that Deng Xiaoping at the same time also remarked that China hadn’t spent enough time studying these treasures and that they needed to do more to protect them. And there has been, throughout this period, a concern that China is import dependent on key commodities, including oil and energy, even food, and that China didn’t want the same to take place in the context of rare earths, which, as China’s own industries were developing, it was clear that these would be really critical for China’s own industries to use. And that remains the case.There was a period in time where analysts in China worried very much about the total dysregulation of this market and that this was a sure pathway to actually using up China’s supply of rare earths. They were “cheap and dirty,” was the reigning slogan, and that there was a concern that rare earths were being sold at the price of quote “cabbage or dirt” and that actually the Western developed countries were keeping their own while depleting China of its rare earths. Now, of course, over time, there were efforts to consolidate this industry, but even as late as 2010, production of rare earths exceeded quotas by more than 35 percent, suggesting that the government really struggled to reign in many of these illegal operations actually in Southern China, and leading some observers to say that the main competition to China were the crime rings inside China’s own borders.And so, that’s about the time at which this 2010 crisis with Japan erupted over disputed islands in the East China Sea. And that was really the first time that there was the temporary reduction in the export of rare earths for political reasons as opposed to concerns about market and disorganization. And it was a wake-up call for Japan and for the world, but it turns out, as we looked further into this, that it wasn’t clearly the result of a strategic decision by Beijing, that in fact, research by the geographer Julie Klinger suggested that actually it was in the context of this geopolitical tiff between Japan and China, that there were actually subnational officials, port administrators that thought that this would be a good way to show China’s displeasure with Japan’s arrest of this drunk fishing captain.And so whatever the reason, I think it was that that I think actually alerted authorities in Beijing that this could indeed be potentially a source of future leverage. But that wasn’t the end of the debate. In fact, there were questions when the first Trump administration took its actions against Huawei, there were some media in China that suggested, “Wow, maybe we should use this kind of rare earth weapon.” But others, more authoritative voices, more sober voices suggested that this was not really likely to be an effective strategy, that actually China continued to depend on international markets and technologies and in fact joint exploration and that using the so-called rare earth weapon prematurely could be counterproductive. And so, it was clearly a process of, over time, learning and desiring greater geopolitical leverage that the Chinese leadership, I think, seized on this, but only really quite late.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI was in government in 2010 when that use of restrictions of rare earths to Japan first I think caught people’s attention in Washington as highlighting the importance of this issue. I think ever since then, there has been lots of talk in American foreign policy circles in the U.S. government about properly diversifying and building up critical minerals, mining and refining capacity in the United States or among U.S. allies. It has not gone that far. I think that’s what we saw in the reaction to Chinese restrictions last year. There’s a new push now. I think the Pax Silica is the State Department’s name for their initiative to build up alternate supply chains. Do you see any evidence that that’s working, that there’s meaningful progress here? I guess to put it a different way, are the Chinese fears that this might be counterproductive and that it will lead to diversification being borne out now?JESSICA CHEN WEISSI think diversification is taking place, but there are so many different potential choke points that it’s hard to see this being resolved anytime soon where the United States will and its allies and partners will emerge immune to future potential Chinese retaliation or threat of retaliation. And in particular, China, this is not just a matter of the raw stuff, it’s the processing and the refining and frankly the know-how that goes into this that is challenging and that China has so many more universities, graduates focused on this set of issues that it may be difficult. But that said, we in the article say that a little diversification goes a long way, and so actually remaining dependent to some extent is not as much of a problem. It’s a problem when it’s overdependent and it actually encourages Chinese hubris or the temptation to continue to weaponize this threat.And so, that then really points to what’s going to happen in September with the upcoming Xi visit. Will that truce be sustained? My sense is that both sides want it to, but there are obviously things that could spoil that. So if the United States wanted to make good on some of its threats to impose secondary sanctions on China over Iran and oil, I mean, there are other things that could upset this pause.DAN KURTZ-PHELANHave you seen similar debates about rare earths dependence on China playing out elsewhere in the world and other capitals outside of Washington? I mean, to what extent is this a uniquely American concern and to what extent is it precipitating a broader shift?JESSICA CHEN WEISSI think it’s very much galvanizing debates around the world. China’s export control restrictions are not only targeted at the United States, they apply to all countries around the world. And there’s a lot of, maybe that’s in fact an own goal. China, in trying to push back against the United States, actually aroused a great deal of fear and concern across the world. I think the other thing is that in Japan, this has been a conversation since 2010, and since 2010, Japan has gone from a 90 percent reliance to something like a 60 percent reliance on the Chinese supply of rare earths and permanent magnets. And also these are intertwined supply chains. So much of what affects Japan also affects the United States. So even though there’s a truce, also the implementation, one of the things that we talk about is how understaffed China’s bureaucracy was at the time that they announced these export restrictions as licensing regime.And so, in some ways they’re building out this capacity both to allow but also restrict these exports and their licenses. So it’s definitely a worldwide conversation and that’s part of why you’ve got so many countries interested in working with the United States to address stable and secure supply chains. But it’s important to note that they aren’t choosing one or the other, right? They’re working with the United States, but they’re also continuing to work with China.DAN KURTZ-PHELANThat own-goal dynamic I think could be applied to Chinese policy across a broader range of areas during Trump’s second term. It’s a time when Trump is doing a lot to alienate U.S. allies and partners and others in a whole variety of ways. It brought to mind a sentence that you wrote in that 2022 piece, “The China Trap,” where you warned that quote, “China sees U.S. leadership as weakened by hypocrisy and neglect, providing an opening to force others to accept its influence and legitimacy.” That seems even truer now than it did back then, but there are a lot of ways that China has perhaps been too heavy-handed in trying to make sense of this opening and thus not picked off allies and partners the way it might. In fact, you see lots of evidence that allies in East Asia and even in Europe at this point are still quite willing to work with Washington when it comes to some of the hard security and economic issues. Do you think that’s the right reading of Chinese policy and how it’s using this moment?JESSICA CHEN WEISSI think there are a couple of drivers of China’s lack of recalibration in ways that would more effectively take advantage of the growing skepticism of the United States. One is that, as I noted, I think Chinese strategists are unsure of how long this pause with the United States will last. And as a result, they are unwilling to put greater distance between China and some of China’s strategic partners that they have worked with in order to provide a degree of insulation and balance against the United States. So I’m thinking about Russia here and China’s closeness with Russia is a leading source of European antagonism and skepticism of China.I think the other source is China’s own domestic economic challenges, and in some ways that is bound up with their, particularly Xi Jinping’s, unwillingness to do more to rebalance internally away from exports as a driver or sustainer of growth and more toward domestic consumption in households. This is partly, I think, an ideological preference and belief, but it’s also a part of why these painful changes have not been as forthcoming. And as you see the growing global pushback to what they’re calling the second China shock, there’s an intransigence there that I think is suggesting that China is focused on other things other than the defenestration of the United States. I mean, the United States is taking itself out of the number one position, but China is not clearly grabbing that brass ring. China is moving much more, looking for opportunities, but I think largely cautious about where this moment leads and not wanting to move too quickly to either assume the global burdens or make the compromises, the concessions, I think, necessary to earn China more trust and goodwill, not just in the United States, but from around the world.We see in the polling that approval of China has picked up in the United States, but especially in other countries. Xi Jinping compares favorably with Donald Trump, but I would say that overall we’re still in . . . minorities look to the Chinese leadership with approval. So China has gained, but I think that trust is still elusive in part for these reasons.DAN KURTZ-PHELANSo the argument implied in my question that China is missing a moment of opportunity, in fact, reflects a view that this is not really as deep a rupture as many of us think to use the now much overused term used by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. That this is more of a pause in structural developments rather than a fundamental change.JESSICA CHEN WEISSNo, I actually think it is a rupture. I just think that China doesn’t see this as a contest for global supremacy, and so it’s not eager to take up and make that dash while the opportunity presents itself. And what I meant by maybe a pause, it’s that the U.S. willingness to be more conciliatory toward China, that they are unsure of whether there will be this snapback that will then result in them, China needing to once again rely on its strategic buffers, if you will.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAre you surprised by both the durability and continuing growth and depth of the Sino-Russian relationship? I think this, over the last few years, surprised lots of observers of that relationship over time, but it seems to be continuing to get deeper and stronger. How do you read those developments?JESSICA CHEN WEISSI mean, I think it comes back to the strategic underpinnings, which is that in a world of U.S. supremacy and willingness to put great pressure on both China and Russia, the two have looked to each other as sources of ballast and insurance. And although I would like to have seen a lessening of that, especially as the United States and China seem to be dialing down their attentions, I think that we would need to see a much more concerted and durable effort to achieve a new modus vivendi to see any sign growing in China, that there is some strategic upside to keeping Russia a bit at a distance. And we haven’t, I think, begun to turn that.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou mentioned the piece that you wrote in 2024 along with Bonnie Glaser and Tom Christensen, that was about Taiwan and the growing risks in the Taiwan Strait. That does seem to be another place where there’s probably a little bit more calm than we worried about a year or two ago, even though a lot of Chinese activities around Taiwan have continued, military activities and other. How do you understand this moment and the cross-strait dynamic?JESSICA CHEN WEISSSo a couple things. First, while I argued that it was unwise for Trump to be making what appeared to be unilateral concessions to China on Taiwan, I think we also can see that China hasn’t exploited what many saw as a lack of credibility and resolve to attack Taiwan. And I think that that reflects a deeper judgment that, as John Culver has said, Taiwan is a crisis to be avoided rather than an opportunity to be seized. And that, of course, China has gone through its own upheaval with the purge of China’s most senior military officers. I think that this is not a China that is itching for war. I think that they have continued their campaign of pressure on Taiwan. They do not like the current president, but to some extent, I think the fact that both the United States and China are a bit less focused on quote-unquote “resolving this issue” at the moment is a good thing.I hope that it continues. Of course, we have elections around the corner in both Taiwan and in the United States, and so we’ll have to see where politics takes us. But ultimately, this is a political question rather than a question of the military balance. And so, even as I think the United States has unwisely spent many of its munitions fighting this war in Iran, I don’t think that the consequences are as immediate as many, I think, fear, those who privilege the military balance as really the only thing holding Xi Jinping back from attacking Taiwan. I don’t see it in that way.DAN KURTZ-PHELANSo the fact that there’s not a U.S. aircraft carrier in the region anymore, that we’ve used up lots of our air defense and other kinds of munitions we would need in that kind of conflict, that’s not going to lead to temptation on Xi Jinping’s part to do something precipitous. That’s a worry we can save for another day.JESSICA CHEN WEISSI’m just saying that the risk may be higher, but it wasn’t so great to begin with that now it has tipped the scales.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI think there’s a sense in the debate that, whereas we used to be very focused on 2027 as the moment of great risk, it’s now 2028 when there’ll be a presidential election in the United States, also one in Taiwan and the chance that DPP, the current ruling party, that has a harder line on relations with mainland China could be reelected. I think the worry that you hear from some analysts is that there’s this moment now when policymakers in Beijing think that events in Taiwan are more or less moving in their direction, that they don’t need to worry about massive changes in the other direction, that could come apart very, very quickly in 2028.
